title: The Score for a Vanishing Sound
logline: A drumming teacher passes on a rhythm as spoken syllables before letting a student near the drum, a way of writing down, in sound, something that happens too fast to watch.

object.note: Object 5 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: The moment-by-moment rhythm of work becomes a rhythm taught aloud: a drumming teacher passing on, in spoken syllables, something too fast to watch.

thread_out.thread: Something too fast to watch becomes something too fast to replay: an umpire's split-second ruling while a whole ground waits in silence.

lesson.in_simple_terms: Some things happen too fast to watch, so people learn them by writing them down in another form. The Abhidhamma does this for a single act of seeing, charting it as a sequence of beats, because no act happens in just one moment.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: ඇසින් අල්ලාගත නොහැකි තරම් වේගවත් දේ ඉගෙන ගන්නේ ඒවා වෙනත් ආකාරයකින් ලියා තබාගෙන වන අතර, එක් දැකීමක්වත් එක් මොහොතකින් සිදු නොවන බැවින් අභිධර්මය එය පියවර පෙළක් ලෙස සටහන් කරයි.
lesson.the_teaching: Margaya states that nothing a person does, whether properly seeing, understanding a word, lifting a hand, giving or taking, happens in a single mind-moment; each needs an ordered series, a cognitive process (vīthi) (C038). Because the mind is too subtle and too fast to examine directly, even students know these processes only by inference, and the texts use charts, marking each mind-moment with dots and a letter, to make the sequence easy to hold in mind (C038, C042). The fullest eye-door process has seventeen moments: the resting mind is disturbed, turns toward the object, sees, receives, investigates, determines, runs seven moments of impulsion and two of registration (C041).
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The teacher recites syllable patterns before the student is allowed near the drum, and the student's halting repetitions slowly become a fluent rhythm. Watching a pattern too quick to follow turned into syllables that can be spoken and remembered, the viewer sees a living version of writing down what is too fast to see, without anyone mentioning charts.

key_terms.en: cognitive process: an ordered series of mind-moments
the seventeen mind-moments of the fullest sense process

lesson.caution: The charts are a traditional teaching notation, not a readout of brain activity, and the seventeen moments are not a timing in milliseconds.
lesson.builds_on: The work film found the same few parts in every moment; this one shows how the texts line those moments up into a sequence that can be learned, the way a rhythm is.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
